checks.claim: Before Linnaeus a species' scientific name was a Latin descriptive phrase (polynomial), and the phrases grew longer as more species were found
checks.note: Wikipedia: a generic name with a specific name 'from one to several words long'; 'as more species were discovered, the names necessarily became longer and unwieldy'. Grokipedia (https://grokipedia.com/page/Binomial_nomenclature) agrees: 'lengthy polynomial descriptions in Latin'.

checks.claim: Linnaeus's 1758 book (Systema Naturae, 10th ed.) names the honey bee Apis mellifera
checks.note: Apis mellifera Linnaeus, 1758, Systema Naturae 10th ed. vol. 1 p. 576 (also https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/c5814455-acdb-4647-a1a6-c1e7c1f94d5e). His later name Apis mellifica (Fauna Suecica, 1761) is an unnecessary replacement; mellifera stands.

checks.claim: The 1758 entry still gives a descriptive phrase: a downy bee with a greyish thorax and a brown abdomen (paraphrase, not in quotation marks)
checks.note: The Latin is 'A. pubescens, thorace subgriseo, abdomine fusco, pedibus posticis glabris utrinque margine ciliatis'; pubescens = downy, subgriseo = greyish, fusco = dusky/dark brown. The stem paraphrases faithfully (dropping the hind-leg clause) and uses no quotation marks, so it is not presented as a quote.

checks.claim: Key: Apis names the genus
checks.note: First part of a binomial is the genus, second the specific epithet.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: Apis is not the species (Apis mellifera as a whole is), not the family (Apidae), not the order (Hymenoptera)
Context: genus capitalised, epithet lower case, both italic; two-word names easier to remember and use and replaced the phrases
checks.note: Wikipedia: trivial names 'were much easier to remember and use than the parallel polynomial names and eventually replaced them'. The context's 'soon' is a fair gloss (the binomials took over within the following decades).

checks.claim: Linnaeus, a Swedish naturalist, put people in one order with apes and monkeys
checks.note: Earlier editions grouped Homo with Simia under Anthropomorpha ('manlike'); the 10th edition replaced it with Primates.

checks.claim: He named the order Primates in 1758, the same year he gave our species the name Homo sapiens
checks.note: Wikipedia: the 10th edition (1758) 'introduced new terms, including Mammalia and Primates, the latter replacing Anthropomorpha', and gave humans 'the full binomial Homo sapiens'. Grokipedia (https://grokipedia.com/page/Carl_Linnaeus) also dates Homo sapiens in Primates to the 10th edition, 1758.

checks.claim: Apes and monkeys went into Simia, people into Homo
checks.note: Wikipedia lists Primates as Homo (humans), Simia (monkeys and apes), Lemur, Vespertilio (bats). A small wrinkle, not needed at grade 7: the 1758 Homo also held Homo troglodytes, a muddled 'cave man' built partly from travellers' tales of apes.

checks.claim: Key: he grouped them by features their bodies share
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'shared anatomical features derived from direct observation and dissection'. Wikipedia (10th edition): he divided the mammals 'based upon the number, situation, and structure of their teeth'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: descent from a shared ancestor (anachronistic, Darwin 1859), habits and diets, lands where they live
checks.note: Linnaeus rejected transmutation; his orders rested on anatomy (teeth), not diet or range.

checks.claim: Context: Linnaeus 'believed every species had been created unchanging'
checks.note: Grokipedia stresses his 'commitment to fixed species concepts', but historians (Wilkins; Amundson via https://johnhawks.net/weblog/topics/history/linnaeus/fixism_linnaeus_amundson_2007.html) note that from about 1744-1751 on he allowed that some new species arise within a genus by hybridization (Peloria). 'Every species ... unchanging' overstates it for the Linnaeus of 1758. Fix: 'he believed species had been made by God and did not descend from one another'.

checks.claim: Context: Darwin's On the Origin of Species, 1859, a century later, explained shared features as descent from common ancestors
checks.note: Published 24 November 1859; 101 years after 1758.

checks.claim: Context: Linnaeus put bats in his Primates
checks.note: Vespertilio (bats) was a genus of his Primates in 1758.

checks.claim: Rose and apple share the family Rosaceae (the smallest principal rank they share)
checks.note: Grokipedia lists apples (Malus) in Rosaceae; Rosa is in subfamily Rosoideae, Malus in Amygdaloideae (tribe Maleae), so among the principal ranks family is the smallest they share.

checks.claim: Rose and stinging nettle share only the order (Rosales)
checks.note: Grokipedia: Urtica dioica is 'class Magnoliopsida, order Rosales, family Urticaceae' (APG IV). Rosaceae is in Rosales (https://grokipedia.com/page/Rosaceae). Under the older Cronquist system nettles were in Urticales, but the modern placement is Rosales.

checks.claim: Rose and Christmas rose share the class (Magnoliopsida) but not order or family
checks.note: Grokipedia: Helleborus niger is Plantae, Tracheophyta, Magnoliopsida, Ranunculales, Ranunculaceae. Rose's class from Grokipedia only by way of Rosales (Grokipedia's Rose and Rosaceae pages name no class; its Urtica dioica page gives Rosales in Magnoliopsida). GBIF (https://gbif.org/species/8395064) gives Rosa as Plantae, Tracheophyta, Magnoliopsida, Rosales, Rosaceae. So the shared class holds.

checks.claim: Rose and moss share only the kingdom
checks.note: Mosses are division/phylum Bryophyta; the rose is Tracheophyta. Kingdom Plantae is the only principal rank shared.

checks.claim: Key: the apple tree is the rose's closest relative; wrong choices nettle, Christmas rose, moss
checks.note: OpenStax: at each sublevel organisms become more similar because more closely related. The stem's own data make the apple the closest.

checks.claim: Context: 'From the largest group to the smallest, the ranks run kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species'
checks.note: Today's largest principal rank is the domain, above the kingdom (and this unit's own Woese question says 'three domains above the kingdoms'). The list is the classic Linnaean ladder, so not false for a plant ladder, but 'from the largest group' clashes with the domain question. Fix: 'From the kingdom down to the smallest group, the ranks run kingdom, phylum, ...'.

checks.claim: Context: the apple shares the rose family; the Christmas rose belongs to the buttercup family
checks.note: Grokipedia: Ranunculaceae, 'the buttercup family'.

checks.claim: Florida panther, Canadian cougar and Chilean puma are all Puma concolor
checks.note: Range 'from the Yukon Territory in Canada to the southern tip of the Andes in Patagonia, Argentina and Chile'; the Florida panther is P. c. coryi (Grokipedia) or part of P. c. couguar under the 2017 Cat Classification Task Force (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cougar).

checks.claim: Key: one species under three names
Wrong choices: three species one per country; three species in the genus Puma; two species one per continent
checks.note: All wrong: one species. The 2017 task force splits it into two subspecies (P. c. couguar, North and Central America; P. c. concolor, South America), but subspecies, not species, so 'two species, one on each continent' stays wrong.

checks.claim: Context: it holds the record for the animal with the most names, over 40 in English alone; cougar, puma, mountain lion, panther, catamount
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'holds the Guinness record for the animal with the greatest number of names, with over 40 in English alone'. Grokipedia says 'mammal', 'over 40 documented common names', and lists mountain lion, puma, panther, catamount.

checks.claim: Key: the lungfish is a true fish (a bony, lobe-finned fish)
checks.note: Grokipedia: Dipnoi within 'the lobe-finned fish group Sarcopterygii', freshwater, lungs 'supplement gill respiration'. Lobe-finned and ray-finned fishes together are the bony fishes (UCL, https://www.ucl.ac.uk/museums-static/obl4he/vertebratediversity/lobefinned_fishes.html).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: cuttlefish is not a fish (cephalopod mollusc; cuttlebone an internal shell)
checks.note: 'marine cephalopod mollusks in the order Sepiida'; 'a distinctive internal calcareous shell known as the cuttlebone'. Squid are fellow Decapodiformes; octopuses are cephalopods too.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: starfish is not a fish (Echinodermata, kin of sea urchins)
checks.note: Marine invertebrates of the phylum Echinodermata; relatives include sea urchins; 'sea star' promoted because they are not fish.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: jellyfish is not a fish (Cnidaria, kin of corals)
checks.note: 'more closely related to corals and sea anemones than to true fish'; no vertebrae, fins or gills.

checks.claim: Stem: 'animals of sea and river'
checks.note: Lungfish are freshwater (Africa, South America, Australia); the other three are marine.

checks.claim: Context: a true fish has a backbone; the lungfish gulps air with lungs as well as breathing with gills; none of the three others has a backbone
checks.note: Grokipedia: lungfish use buccal pumping to breathe air and the lungs supplement the gills (adult gills reduced in some species). All three others are invertebrates.

checks.claim: Key logic: broad leaves -> 3; alternate leaves -> oak
checks.note: Following the key as written, broad + alternating leaves reach 3b, oak. A dichotomous key is 'a series of paired statements, called couplets, where each pair presents two mutually exclusive alternatives'.

checks.claim: Oak leaves alternate and are often lobed
checks.note: 'Leaves are alternate, simple, and petiolate'; 'often lobed or toothed and alternate along the branches'.

checks.claim: Maple leaves grow in opposite pairs and are often lobed
checks.note: 'arranged oppositely on the stems'; 'typically simple and palmately lobed with 3 to 5 lobes'.

checks.claim: Pine needles in bundles of two to five
checks.note: 'Each fascicle contains 2 to 5 needles (rarely 1 or up to 6)'.

checks.claim: Spruce needles grow singly
checks.note: 'attached singly to the twigs via short, peg-like projections (pulvini)'.

checks.claim: Context: two contrasting choices at each step, each leading to the next step or a name
Robert Whittaker, American plant ecologist, five kingdoms in 1969
checks.note: 'an American plant ecologist'; proposed 'the Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Protista, and Monera in 1969'.

checks.claim: He told the many-celled kingdoms apart mainly by how their members feed
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'based mainly upon differences in nutrition'; Plantae 'mostly multicellular autotrophs', Fungi 'multicellular saprotrophs', Animalia 'multicellular heterotrophs'. Grokipedia (https://grokipedia.com/page/Kingdom_(biology)): 'autotrophic via photosynthesis, absorptive heterotrophy, or ingestive heterotrophy'.

checks.claim: Key: a many-celled creature that takes food in and digests it inside is placed among the animals
checks.note: Animals are 'multicellular eukaryotic ingestive heterotrophs'. A sessile reef animal (coral, sponge) fits.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: plants (make own food), fungi (absorb food digested outside), protists (Whittaker's protists are mainly one-celled; the creature is many-celled)
checks.note: Fungi 'secrete digestive enzymes externally' and absorb; 'unlike phagotrophic animals that ingest food particles'.

checks.claim: Context: the five kingdoms named; plants make food, fungi absorb food broken down outside, animals take food in and digest it inside; staying in one place does not make a thing a plant
Methanogens live in wetlands and the guts of cattle
checks.note: Wetlands, sediments and 'the digestive tracts of ruminants'.

checks.claim: They look like bacteria: single cells with no nucleus; at first counted as bacteria
checks.note: 'unicellular organisms lacking a membrane-bound nucleus'; cocci and rods; 'initially classified as bacteria'; methanogens 'provisionally assigned to the bacterial domain based on phenotypic traits'.

checks.claim: Carl Woese and George Fox, University of Illinois, compared ribosomal RNA; published 1977
checks.note: Woese on the Illinois faculty from 1964; with George E. Fox compared 16S rRNA oligonucleotide catalogs; 1977 PNAS paper found methanogens a distinct group, unlike eubacteria or eukaryotes ('archaebacteria', a third primary kingdom).

checks.claim: Key: a separate branch of life; wrong choices: unusual bacteria (the pre-1977 view), ancestors of all bacteria, one-celled fungus
checks.note: 16S rRNA showed 'a distinct, deeply branching group'; none of the distractors is what the comparison showed.

checks.claim: Context: many scientists doubted it at first; in 1990 Woese proposed three domains above the kingdoms: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya
checks.note: 'substantial initial resistance'; 1990 PNAS with Otto Kandler and Mark Wheelis, 'proposal for the domains Archaea, Bacteria, and Eucarya'. 'Woese proposed' is a fair short form.

checks.claim: Baker's yeast, a fern and a person are all Eukarya
checks.note: Yeasts, plants and animals are eukaryotes.

checks.claim: Key: 'Cells that each hold a nucleus'
checks.note: The word 'each' makes it false for the person: mature mammalian red blood cells are anucleate (Grokipedia Red blood cell; Grokipedia Eukaryote: 'mature mammalian red blood cells extrude their nucleus during development'), and they are about 84% of a person's cells by count (Sender et al. 2016, https://bionumbers.hms.harvard.edu/bionumber.aspx?id=113005). Many 7th graders are taught this. True statement: eukaryotes are organisms whose cells contain a membrane-bound nucleus. Fix: key 'Cells built with a nucleus' or 'Cells with a nucleus', and add to the context: 'A person's red blood cells lose their nucleus as they mature, but they begin with one.'

checks.claim: Wrong choice: bodies built of many cells (yeast is one-celled)
checks.note: Baker's yeast lives as single cells (it buds).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: cells with a stiff outer wall (a person's cells have none)
checks.note: Plants and fungi have walls; walls are absent in animal cells.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: making food from light (only the fern)
Context: Eukarya keep their genetic material in a nucleus, from one-celled yeasts and amoebas to plants, fungi and animals; bacteria and archaea have none
checks.note: 'organisms whose cells contain a membrane-bound nucleus that encloses their genetic material'.

checks.claim: Linnaeus placed the tomato in Solanum, beside the potato, in 1753
checks.note: Solanum lycopersicum, Species Plantarum 1753.

checks.claim: Philip Miller, chief gardener of the Chelsea Physic Garden in London
checks.note: 'chief gardener at the Chelsea Physic Garden for nearly 50 years from 1722'.

checks.claim: Miller 'soon moved it into a genus of its own, Lycopersicon'
checks.note: Miller did move the tomato out of Solanum: genus Lycopersicon Mill. 1754 (Gardeners Dictionary abridged ed. 4, https://www.ipni.org/n/30022251-2), species Lycopersicon esculentum 1768. But his Lycopersicon was not the tomato's own: in the 8th edition (1768) he put the potato in it too, as Lycopersicon tuberosum (L.) Mill. (IPNI 816719-1, basionym Solanum tuberosum L.), alongside L. peruvianum (https://www.ipni.org/n/816705-1). So Miller did not part the tomato from the potato, which is what the stem's story (and the key 'the potato's genus') implies; tomatoes-only Lycopersicon apart from the potato was the usage of later botanists (e.g. Dunal 1816 treated tomatoes as a separate genus Lycopersicon: Tepe et al. 2016). Wikipedia's 'its own genus' oversimplifies. Fix: 'Philip Miller ... soon moved it out of Solanum into the genus Lycopersicon, and for two centuries botanists kept the tomatoes there, apart from the potato.'

checks.claim: Key: DNA shows the tomato belongs in the potato's genus (Solanum)
checks.note: 'Genetic evidence shows that Linnaeus was correct to put the tomato in the genus Solanum'; tomato and potato 'forming a tight clade within Solanum'. Grokipedia Tomato: 'molecular evidence has supported its reclassification into Solanum'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: a genus of its own; the tobacco plant's genus (Nicotiana); a family of its own
checks.note: DNA 'confirms Lycopersicon as a clade' nested in the potato lineage of Solanum, so a separate genus would leave Solanum paraphyletic; tobacco is another genus of the same family Solanaceae.

checks.claim: Context: tomato and potato very close relatives within Solanum; the tomato is Solanum lycopersicum again; DNA tests groupings made by eye

unit_notes: 6 ok, 2 error, 2 uncertain. Errors: (1) 2a5eea9f40 key 'Cells that each hold a nucleus' is false for a person (mature red blood cells, ~84% of human cells, have no nucleus); drop 'each'. (2) e95051e8ca: Miller's Lycopersicon was not a genus of the tomato's own; his 1768 edition put the potato in it too (Lycopersicon tuberosum, IPNI 816719-1); reword so later botanists, not Miller, kept tomatoes apart from the potato. Uncertain: 4641c08f0e context 'believed every species had been created unchanging' (later Linnaeus allowed hybrid species within a genus; soften to 'made by God, not descended from one another'); 18027e1f85 context 'From the largest group ... kingdom' clashes with this unit's domains above kingdoms (say 'From the kingdom down'). Honey bee Latin is paraphrased faithfully and not in quotation marks. Anthropomorpha (earlier editions, e.g. 6th ed. 1748) became Primates in the 10th ed. 1758; Primates held Homo, Simia, Lemur and bats. Rose ranks all check (apple: Rosaceae; nettle: Rosales; Christmas rose: class Magnoliopsida via Grokipedia's Helleborus niger and Urtica dioica pages, GBIF for Rosa; moss: Bryophyta).
